about: Questions John has said the site must answer. Each one is tested by probes: multiple-choice questions a newcomer should be able to answer from the site. A probe with evidence is answered on the built site, and CI checks that it stays answered. A probe with no evidence yet is a gap the next goal audit turns into a ticket. See README.md.
not_sure: Not sure / the site doesn't say

questions.asked: how does the UK tax, debt and spending compare to other major nations
questions.reading: Major nations is read as the G7 (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK and the US), with the wider OECD as context. Tax and spending are compared as a share of GDP; debt as general government gross debt as a share of GDP. Bond markets are read as government borrowing costs (10-year government bond yields) and debt interest paid as a share of GDP, compared with the G7. Yields reflect several things (central bank rates, expected inflation, how much is being borrowed and investors' view of risk), so the site should show them and explain what moves them without presenting them as a verdict on any government.

probes.question: In 2024, how did total UK tax, as a share of the economy (GDP), compare with France, Germany and Italy?

options.C: Higher than Germany but lower than France and Italy
options.D: About the same as all three

probes.why: International page, 2024: UK 34.4% of GDP, against France 43.5%, Italy 42.8% and Germany 38.0%.

evidence.text: France 43.5%
Italy 42.8%
Germany 38.0%
United Kingdom 34.4%

probes.question: In 2024, how did UK government spending, as a share of GDP, compare with the United States and France?

options.C: Higher than the United States, lower than France
options.D: Lower than the United States, higher than France

probes.why: International page, 2024: UK 46.2% of GDP, United States 39.6%, France 57.3%.

evidence.text: United Kingdom 46.2%
United States 39.6%
France 57.3%

probes.question: How does UK government debt, as a share of GDP, compare with the other G7 countries in the latest year shown?

options.B: Higher than most of the G7, lower only than Japan
options.C: Lower than most of the G7, higher only than Germany

probes.why: Borrowing page, IMF figures for 2024: UK 101.3% of GDP, below Japan, Italy, the United States, France and Canada, above Germany (63.9%). The OECD's market-value measure gives the same order.

evidence.text: In 2024, UK government debt was 101.3% of GDP, the second lowest of the seven G7 countries: lower than Japan, Italy, the United States, France and Canada and higher than Germany.

probes.question: Where does the UK rank among the G7 countries on tax as a share of GDP, and on spending?

options.C: Second lowest on tax (of the six with a figure) and fourth highest of seven on spending
options.D: Second highest on tax and lowest on spending

probes.why: International page, 2024: UK tax 34.4% of GDP, above only the United States among the six G7 countries with a figure (Japan not yet published); spending 46.2%, below France, Italy and Germany.

evidence.text: UK taxes were the second lowest as a share of GDP among the G7 (of the 6 with a figure for that year)
UK government spending was the fourth highest in 2024

probes.question: In the latest year shown, does the UK government pay more or less to borrow for 10 years than the other G7 governments?

options.A: More than every other G7 government
options.B: Less than every other G7 government
options.C: About the same as the G7 average

probes.why: Borrowing page: in 2025, the latest full year, the UK's 10-year yield averaged 4.58%, the highest of the G7; in the latest month, September 2026, it was 5.24%, also the highest.

evidence.text: In 2025, the latest full year, the market rate (yield) for new 10-year UK government borrowing averaged 4.58% a year, the highest of the G7.
The latest month, September 2026, was 5.24%, the highest of the G7.

probes.question: How does the interest the UK government pays on its debt, as a share of GDP, compare with the other G7 countries?

options.B: The third highest: below the United States and Italy

probes.why: Borrowing page, OECD figures for 2024: UK net interest 2.2% of GDP, below the United States (4.2%) and Italy (3.6%), above France, Canada, Germany and Japan; 5.5% of revenue, also third highest.

evidence.text: In 2024, the UK government's interest payments, after subtracting interest it received, were 2.2% of GDP, the third highest of the G7: lower than the United States and Italy and higher than France, Canada, Germany and Japan.

probes.question: According to the site, which of these affect what a government pays to borrow?

options.A: Only how well the government runs the economy
options.B: Only the Bank of England's interest rate
options.C: Several things together, including central bank interest rates, expected inflation, how much the government borrows and how much risk investors see
options.D: Nothing: the government sets its own rate

probes.why: Borrowing page section 'What affects what a government pays to borrow?', with the Debt Management Office and OBR quoted word for word.

evidence.text: The UK Debt Management Office, which sells gilts for the government, names several things that move gilt prices, and so yields (quoted in full below):
Different yields can reflect different central bank rates and inflation, not only how investors judge each government.

questions.asked: Have labour kept their electiion manifesto?
questions.source: John, project chat, 2026-11-04 (question 7 of his list of ten)
questions.reading: Read as whether Labour has kept the pledges in its 2024 manifesto that concern public money and everyday costs: tax, the fiscal rules, defence, housing, the NHS and home energy. Where the wording allows more than one reading (for example "taxes on working people", "basic, higher or additional rates" and the debt measure in the fiscal rules), the site shows each reading and its result, and does not pick one.

probes.question: What did Labour’s 2024 manifesto say it would not increase?

options.A: National Insurance, the basic, higher and additional rates of Income Tax, and VAT
options.B: Council tax, business rates and stamp duty
options.C: Only the basic rate of Income Tax
options.D: Nothing: the manifesto made no tax promises

probes.why: Manifesto, page 21: it will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT. The pledge is about tax on working people.

evidence.text: which is why we will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT.

probes.question: Has the government changed the standard VAT rate of 20% since Labour took office?

options.C: No, the standard rate is still 20%

probes.why: The standard rate has stayed at 20%. Budgets changed some reliefs and private school fees, not the standard rate (Full Fact, 28 November 2025).

evidence.text: The standard rate of VAT is still 20%.

probes.question: Have the basic, higher and additional income tax rates on earnings changed since Labour took office?

options.B: Yes, only the additional rate rose

probes.why: The earnings rates are 20%, 40% and 45%, unchanged. The rates on dividends, savings and property income did change (HMRC, Budget 2025).

evidence.text: The basic, higher and additional rates on earnings are still 20%, 40% and 45%

probes.question: What did Budget 2025 do to income tax on dividends, savings and property income?

options.C: Raised the rates: dividends from April 2026, savings and property from April 2027

probes.why: HMRC: dividend ordinary and upper rates rise from 6 April 2026; savings and property rates rise from April 2027 (Budget 2025).

evidence.text: Dividend rates rose from April 2026, and savings and property rates rise from April 2027.

probes.question: Why do readers disagree on whether the National Insurance pledge was kept?

options.A: The manifesto does not say whether it covers employer as well as employee contributions
options.B: Labour never mentioned National Insurance in its manifesto
options.C: The rate was cut, which the manifesto ruled out
options.D: The pledge only covered the first year

probes.why: The manifesto mentions National Insurance once. It does not say whether the pledge covers employer contributions, so the government and critics read it differently (Full Fact, 14 October 2024).

evidence.text: It does not say whether the pledge covers employer contributions as well as employee ones

probes.question: Did Budget 2025 extend the freeze on income tax and National Insurance thresholds?

options.A: No, it ended in April 2028 as planned

probes.why: Budget 2025 extended the freeze by three years, from April 2028 to April 2031 (Budget 2025 speech; Full Fact, 26 November 2025).

evidence.text: extended the freeze on income tax and National Insurance thresholds for three more years, to April 2031.

probes.question: Did Labour’s private school VAT measure take effect, and when?
probes.why: VAT at the standard rate applied to private school fees from 1 January 2025 (Full Fact, 28 May 2026).

evidence.text: VAT at the standard rate of 20% has applied to private school fees since 1 January 2025.

probes.question: What did Labour’s manifesto promise on defence spending?

options.A: To set out the path to spending 2.5% of GDP on defence
options.B: To cut defence spending to 2% of GDP

probes.why: Manifesto, Strong foundations (pages 14 to 22): it will set out the path to spending 2.5% of GDP on defence. The government set 2.5% from April 2027 in February 2025.

evidence.text: we will set out the path to spending 2.5 per cent of GDP on defence.

probes.question: How many net additional homes does the government estimate were added in England from 9 July 2024 to 20 September 2026, against the 1.5 million target?

options.B: About 1.5 million, so the target is met

probes.why: GOV.UK housing supply indicators, April to June 2026: 437,900 estimated net additional homes, 29% of 1.5 million. The 208,600 figure is the official count for 2024-25 only.

evidence.text: The government estimates 437,900 net additional homes in England between 9 July 2024 and 20 September 2026: 29% of the 1.5 million target.

probes.question: In August 2026, what share of waiting pathways for consultant-led NHS treatment had waited up to 18 weeks?
probes.why: NHS England, RTT statistics for August 2026, published 8 October 2026: 65.2% within 18 weeks, against the 92% standard.

evidence.text: In August 2026, 65.2% of the 7.4 million waiting pathways for consultant-led treatment had waited up to 18 weeks.
